source_text: Sed enim cum conuersatio diuinae disciplinae non factis tantum, uerum etiam uerbis periclitetur (nam sicut scriptum est, ecce homo et facta eius, ita, ex ore tuo iustificaberis), meminisse debemus etiam in uerbis quoque idololatriae incursum praecauendum aut de consuetudinis uitio aut timiditatis. deos nationum nominari lex prohibet non utique: nomina eorum pronuntiemus, quae nobis ut dicamus conuersatio extorquet. nam id plerumque dicendum est: in templo Aesculapii illum habes, et, in uico Isidis habito, et sacerdos Iouis factus est, et multa alia in hunc modum, quando et hominibus hoc genus nomina inducuntur. neque enim Saturnum honoro, si ita uocauero eum suo nomine; tam non honoro, quam Marcum, si uocauero Marcum. sed ait: nomen aliorum deorum ne commemoremini neque audiatur de tuo ore. hoc praecepit, ne deos uocemus illos. nam et in prima parte legis, non sumes, inquit, nomen domini dei tui in uano idest idolo. cecidit igitur in idololatriam qui idolum nomine dei honorauerit. quodsi deos dicendum erit, adiciendum est aliquid quo appareat, quia non ego illos deos dico. nam et scriptura deos nominat, sed adicit suos uel nationum; sicut Dauid, cum deos nominasset, ubi ait, dei autem nationum daemonia. sed hoc mihi ad sequentia magis praestructum est. ceterum consuetudinis uitium est Mehercule dicere, Medius Fidius, accedente ignorantia quorundam, qui ignorant iusiurandum esse per Herculem. porro quid erit deieratio per eos quos eierasti quam praeuaricatio fidei cum idololatria? quis enim, per quos deierat, non honorat?
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that idolatry can be committed not only by deeds but also by words, including naming pagan gods and swearing by them.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed, since the conduct of divine discipline is endangered not only by deeds, but also by words (for as it is written, behold the man and his deeds, so, from your mouth you will be justified), we ought to remember that also in words the assault of idolatry must be guarded against, either from the fault of custom or of timidity. The law forbids the gods of the nations to be named, not at all so that we should pronounce their names, which conversation forces us to say. For this must often be said: you have him in the temple of Aesculapius, and, I live in the street of Isis, and he has been made a priest of Jupiter, and many other things in this manner, when also names of this kind are given to men. For I do not honor Saturn, if I have called him by his own name; I do not honor him, just as I do not honor Marcus, if I have called him Marcus. But he says: the name of other gods do not commemorate, nor let it be heard from your mouth. He commanded this, that we should not call them gods. For also in the first part of the law, you shall not take, he says, the name of the Lord your God in vain, that is, for an idol. Therefore he has fallen into idolatry who has honored an idol with the name of God. But if gods must be said, something must be added by which it appears that I do not call them gods. For also Scripture names gods, but adds its own or of the nations; as David, when he had named gods, where he says, but the gods of the nations are demons. But this has been built up by me rather for what follows. For the rest, it is a fault of custom to say by Hercules, by the god of faith, with the ignorance of some approaching, who do not know that it is an oath by Hercules. Furthermore, what will swearing by those whom you have renounced be except a violation of faith with idolatry? For who does not honor those by whom he swears?

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of conversatio as way of life or conduct, and disciplina as the Christian rule of life per the glossary.
rejected: the practice of the divine teaching

choices.why: Literal rendering; the glossary maps nationes to pagans, but here the phrase is a fixed biblical expression, so 'nations' preserves the scriptural echo.
Medius Fidius is a Roman oath deity; rendering it literally as 'the god of faith' preserves the oath formula while making the idolatrous reference clear.
Praevaricatio means a deliberate breach or transgression; 'violation of faith' captures the betrayal of the baptismal commitment.
Eiero specifically means to renounce by oath, which fits the baptismal renunciation of the devil and his works.

pass_b_english: But since the conduct of divine discipline is endangered not only by deeds but also by words—for as it is written, "Behold the man and his deeds," so also "by your mouth you will be justified"—we must remember that the assault of idolatry in words must also be guarded against, whether from the fault of habit or of timidity. The law forbids naming the gods of the pagans, not that we should never pronounce their names when our way of life forces us to speak them. For often one must say: "You have him in the temple of Aesculapius," or "I live on the street of Isis," or "He has been made a priest of Jupiter," and many other things of this kind, since names of this sort are even given to people. For I do not honor Saturn if I call him by his own name, any more than I honor Marcus if I call him Marcus. But it says: "Do not mention the name of other gods, nor let it be heard from your mouth" (Exodus 23:13). He commanded this so that we should not call them gods. For in the first part of the law he says, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Exodus 20:7)—that is, for an idol. So whoever honors an idol with the name of God has fallen into idolatry. But if gods must be spoken of, something must be added to make clear that I do not call them gods. For Scripture also names gods, but adds "their own" or "of the nations," as David did when he named gods, saying, "But the gods of the pagans are demons" (Psalm 96:5; Psalm 95:5 in the Septuagint). But this has been built up more for what follows. As for the rest, it is a fault of habit to say "By Hercules" or "By Medius Fidius," with the ignorance of some who do not know that it is an oath by Hercules. What will swearing by those you have renounced be but a violation of faith with idolatry? For who does not honor those by whom he swears?

problems.why: This is not from Matthew 12:37; it appears to be an allusion to scriptural language about a person and their deeds, not a specific NT citation.
problems.fix: Remove the citation (Matthew 12:37) or leave the quotation uncited.
problems.ruling: Latin cites "ecce homo et facta eius" but attributes it to Matthew 12:37, which does not contain that phrase.

problems.why: Medius Fidius is a Roman oath formula meaning 'by the god Medius Fidius' (a deity of trust/faith), not 'by the god of faith.'
problems.ruling: Latin "Medius Fidius" is a proper deity name; translating as "god of faith" misrepresents the specific oath formula.

fixed: Removed the Matthew 12:37 citation: the source phrase 'ecce homo et facta eius' is not a direct New Testament citation, and the following 'ex ore tuo iustificaberis' is the actual scriptural allusion.
Changed 'By the god of faith' to 'By Medius Fidius': the source 'Medius Fidius' is a Roman oath formula invoking the deity Medius Fidius, not a generic 'god of faith.'

problems.why: Same concept (non-Christians) rendered as 'nations,' 'pagans,' and 'outsiders' interchangeably.
problems.fix: Use 'pagans' consistently or note that 'nations' = pagans.

fixed: The speaker problem for 'By Hercules' is not a real issue: the source simply lists examples of customary oaths without attributing them to a speaker, and the English correctly renders this as a fault of habit.
The mistranslation problem for 'in an idol' is real: the source has 'idolo' (dative/ablative), meaning 'for an idol' or 'to an idol', not 'in an idol'. Changed to 'for an idol'.
The wrong_scripture problem for 'Behold the man and his deeds' is not a real issue: the source does not cite a specific book, and the English correctly leaves it as an unattributed quotation.

The wrong_scripture problem for 'by your mouth you will be justified' is not a real issue: the source has 'ex ore tuo iustificaberis' (from your mouth you will be justified), and the English renders this accurately without adding a citation.

The wrong_scripture problem for 'But the gods of the pagans are demons' is not a real issue: the source has 'dei autem nationum daemonia' (but the gods of the nations are demons), and the English correctly renders 'nationum' as 'pagans' per the glossary.
The wrong_scripture problem for the Psalm citation is not a real issue: the English already gives both Hebrew and Septuagint numbering, which is accurate and clear.
